newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Ferries spared as French dockers strike.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ferries spared as French dockers strike.

text.p: French dockers disrupted key ports with a one-day strike on Monday, for guarantees on pay, fewer hours and early retirement, unions and employers said.
France's largest ports of Le Havre and Marseille were hit, as were about eight others including busy channel ports Calais, Boulogne and Cherbourg, the UNIM French ports association said.
The strike from midnight (2200 GMT Sunday) was aimed mainly at commercial traffic. Tourists were able to travel freely on cross-channel ferries between Britain and France.
Dockers at six ports including Dunkirk, St Nazaire and St Malo voted not to join the strike, UNIM said. Traffic at Rouen, Europe's biggest grain port, was reduced for one hour.
The Communist-backed CGT union, which called the strike, could not confirm how many of its branches had participated.
A union official accused employers of refusing to negotiate on its demands for early retirement at 55 and a reduction in the working week to 35 hours without loss of pay.
A cut in the average working week to 35 hours from 39 over five years is a key policy of the newly elected Socialist-led government, which includes three Communist ministers.
The strike was also called over demands for improvements in guaranteed minimum pay for France's 4,100 dockers.
UNIM denied in a statement it had refused negotiations.
French ports have seen dozens of sporadic disputes since 1991 when a bid to withdraw privileges for dockers sparked a six-month series of 32 strikes costing one billion francs.
The number of registered French dockers has fallen by nearly two thirds from more than 11,000 since the start of this decade.
France's mainly independent ports handle around 300 million tonnes of goods a year.
